newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran-Russia sign accord affecting nuclear deals.
newsitem.headline: Iran-Russia sign accord affecting nuclear deals.

text.p: Russia and Iran on Monday signed a memorandum of understanding on export controls, a step that could help protect Moscow from international criticism of its nuclear cooperation with the Islamic republic.
Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati and his visiting counterpart Yevgeny Primakov signed the document.
"This MOU shows that Russia and Iran observe internationally accepted norms and nobody could condemn the two countries," Primakov told a news conference before leaving at the end of a two-day visit.

Russia has signed an $800 million deal with Iran to complete a nuclear power plant in the southern port of Bushehr despite U.S. objections that Tehran might use the technology to develop nuclear arms. Iran has denied the charge, saying its nuclear sites are open to international inspection.

"Export control is a technical term that refers to cooperation in the international arena in order to ensure non- proliferation of weapons of mass destruction," an Iranian foreign ministry expert told Reuters.
"It also ensures that peaceful technology will not be diverted to such weapons," he said.

Iran and Russia have good ties and earlier this month signed an agreement to expand economic cooperation. Tehran agreed to buy tens of millions of dollars worth of Russian subway cars and technical equipment.
Primakov said cooperation with Iran not only helped both countries but "served regional stability and peace."
He said Iran and Russia were cooperating to try and settle conflicts in Afghanistan and the former Soviet republic of Tajikistan.

Talks between Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov and the republic's armed Islamic opposition began in Moscow on Friday to halt four years of conflict. Representatives from the United Nations and Russia attended.
"Right now, an agreement is being signed in Moscow between the Tajik government and a united opposition...The role of Iran and Russia here is definitely important," Primakov said.
Velayati and Primakov, in a joint statement on Afghanistan, "condemned open violations of human rights and persecution of individuals for political and ethnic reasons."
"The two ministers invite the warring sides in Afgahnistan to stop military operations and encourage them to restore national reconciliation."
The militant Moslem group Taleban overran the Afghan capital in September and now controls 75 percent of the country. They have imposed their strict vision of Islamic law on areas they control.
